questions.question: How do you create a map in Go, and what happens if you write to a nil map?
questions.title: Create A Map In Go, And What
questions.direct_answer: make(map[string]int) or a literal map[string]int{"a": 1}. A nil map reads fine (zero values) but writes panic: assignment to entry in nil map.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Maps Make And Literal beyond memorized syntax.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: make(map[string]int) or a literal map[string]int{"a": 1}. A nil map reads fine (zero values) but writes panic: assignment to entry in nil map.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Two working ways: the make form for runtime-populated maps, and the literal form when the initial contents are known at code time.

```go
m := make(map[string]int)          // empty, ready for writes
m["count"] = 3

defaults := map[string]int{        // starts with contents
    "retries": 3,
    "timeout": 30,
}
```

And one broken way: declaring the var and writing before initializing.

```go
var m map[string]int               // nil — header exists, no buckets
m["k"] = 1                          // panic: assignment to entry in nil map
```

The asymmetry surprises people: reads on that same nil map work fine — a lookup returns the zero value, len is 0, range runs zero iterations. Only the write panics. The why: a map value is a pointer to a hash structure; nil points at nothing, so a write has nowhere to put the entry, while a read of 'nothing' can honestly answer 'not present, here's your zero value.'

So the rule is simple: make() (or a literal) before any write. Reads on nil are safe; the panic is write-only, and it's the most common map runtime error in beginner Go.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why the write-only panic? Look at what the two operations need:

A read asks 'is there an entry with key k, and what's its value?' On a nil map, the honest answer is 'no such entry' — which the runtime expresses as (zero value, not-present). No structure needed; absence is expressible without storage.

A write asks 'put this entry somewhere findable.' That needs a bucket array, hash seeds, growth machinery — the whole map structure that make() allocates. With a nil pointer to that structure, there's nowhere to put it. Panic is the runtime refusing to pretend.

The comparison with slices clarifies the design: a nil slice CAN be appended to, because append's allocate-path creates the backing storage on demand — a slice header alone is enough to start. A map can't be lazily created because the map value is a pointer to an ALREADY-COMPLETE structure; there's no 'grow into it' path the way a slice header grows into its array. So var s []int; s = append(s, x) is fine, var m map[string]int; m[x] = 1 panics — the asymmetry is structural, not arbitrary.

The bug pattern it creates: passing a nil map into a function that populates it. The fix is return-the-map (the function makes and returns it) rather than fill-the-parameter — which is also just cleaner Go.

questions.question: make(map) with capacity hint — what does it do?
questions.title: Make(map) With Capacity Hint — What Does
questions.direct_answer: make(map[K]V, n) pre-allocates roughly n entries' worth of buckets. A performance hint only — the map grows past n without error.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Maps Make And Literal.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: make(map[K]V, n) pre-allocates roughly n entries' worth of buckets. A performance hint only — the map grows past n without error.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The size argument in make(map[K]V, n) is a capacity hint, not a limit. It tells the runtime 'I expect about n entries — size the initial bucket structure for that,' avoiding the early growth-and-rehash cycles as the map fills from zero.

The hint is purely advisory. Exceed it and the map grows normally — no error, no truncation, no visible difference except allocation timing. Undershoot it (hint 1000, use 10) and you've wasted some memory up front; the runtime doesn't refund it.

When it matters: maps that will definitely hold a known-count set — building a lookup from a slice of length n (hint n), a count-by-key aggregation over known input. For small maps or unknown sizes, the hint buys nothing measurable; the default growth handles small maps in one allocation anyway.

And note the contrast with slices: make([]T, n) on a slice makes n ELEMENTS (zeroed, len n). make(map, n) makes capacity for n entries but zero entries exist. The same function name, two different size semantics — the slice's number is a length, the map's is a hint.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
What the hint controls is the initial bucket count. A Go map is a hash table: an array of buckets, each holding ~8 entries, with overflow chaining and incremental rehashing on growth. From empty, the first inserts trigger several grow-rehash steps as the entry count crosses thresholds — cheap individually, but a loop inserting 100k entries into an unhinted map pays for every growth along the way.

make(map[string]int, 100_000) pre-sizes the bucket array for ~100k entries — the growth steps happen once at allocation instead of during the fill loop. For big, size-knowable builds that's a real win; benchmarks show it clearly at six-figure sizes.

The '~' in 'roughly n buckets' matters: the runtime computes the bucket count from n via its own formula (n/8 buckets, rounded per growth class), so hint 100 doesn't allocate exactly 100 slots' worth — it allocates the size class that fits. That's fine; the hint is an input to a heuristic, not an exact reservation.

The debugging lesson it encodes: map performance issues are usually allocation/rehash churn, visible in profiling as runtime.makemap and growth allocations. When a profile shows that, the hint is the fix; when it doesn't, adding hints is noise.

questions.question: Map literal vs make — when each?
questions.title: Map Literal Vs Make — When Each
questions.direct_answer: Literal when initial pairs are static: map[string]int{"retries": 3}. make when populated at runtime or when you want the capacity hint.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Maps Make And Literal.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Literal when initial pairs are static: map[string]int{"retries": 3}. make when populated at runtime or when you want the capacity hint.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Deep Dive
sections.content:
The two forms differ in when their contents exist — and that decides everything else. A literal is fully constructed before any code runs: keys hashed, buckets laid out, entries stored, at program init for package-level literals. That's why fixed lookups (status codes, default configs, enum-to-string tables) are literals — the data is as static as the code, and initializing it once at startup is free.

make() constructs the same machinery but empty: buckets for zero-or-hinted entries, filled by whatever the program discovers at runtime. The contents are data-driven — parsed input, counted events, cached results — so they can't be a literal even if you wanted them to be.

The empty literal map[string]int{} is the bridge between the forms: a literal with zero entries, fully initialized, immediately writable. It's the idiomatic answer to 'I need a write-ready map and have nothing to prefill' — and its existence is why the nil-map panic is always a var-declaration mistake, never a necessity: write-ready is one {} away.

The style signal to read in code review: literals whose values change operationally (feature flags updated at runtime, limits read from config files) are config that outgrew its form — the moment values change without code changes, they belong in loaded data, and the literal is the migration debt.

questions.question: What are the zero values in a Go map?
questions.title: Re The Zero Values In A Go
questions.direct_answer: A missing key returns the VALUE TYPE's zero value: m["missing"] is 0, "", or false — not an error. The comma-ok idiom distinguishes stored-zero from missing.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Maps Make And Literal.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: A missing key returns the VALUE TYPE's zero value: m["missing"] is 0, "", or false — not an error. The comma-ok idiom distinguishes stored-zero from missing.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Map lookups never fail on a missing key — they return the zero value of the value type. A missing int key gives 0; a missing string gives ""; a missing bool gives false; a missing struct value gives the struct with all fields zeroed. The two-valued lookup distinguishes present from absent:

```go
v := m["maybe"]            // 0 if absent, or if stored 0 — ambiguous
v, ok := m["maybe"]       // ok: false → absent; true → present (even if v is 0)
```

The single-value form is a feature for counting and accumulating — m[w]++ works whether w exists (increments) or not (0+1=1) — but it's a trap for presence-sensitive logic: checking 'did they opt in?' via `if m[optin]` breaks when false is a valid stored answer.

The comma-ok form is the precise instrument: it answers presence and value as separate facts. Use it whenever a stored zero value is legitimate data — optional fields, flags that start false, sparse counters at 0.

The interface to internalize: a map lookup is total — every key gives an answer. The zero value isn't an error signal; it's just the default. When you need to distinguish 'default because absent' from 'explicitly the default,' that's what ok is for.

questions.question: How do map keys work — what types can be keys?
questions.title: Map Keys Work — What Types Can
questions.direct_answer: Any comparable type: strings, ints, bools, arrays, structs of comparables, pointers, interfaces. NOT slices, maps, or functions — they have no ==.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Maps Make And Literal.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Any comparable type: strings, ints, bools, arrays, structs of comparables, pointers, interfaces. NOT slices, maps, or functions — they have no ==.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A key type must support equality, because a hash table needs to (1) hash the key and (2) compare a probed key against the stored one. Anything with == defined can be a key: strings, all numeric types, bools, pointers, channels, interfaces, arrays, and structs whose fields are all comparable.

What can't: slices, maps, and functions. == is not defined for them (comparing two slices can't answer 'same contents?' cheaply and Go refuses reference-vs-content ambiguity), so they can't hash or match. A struct containing a slice field inherits the restriction — no == for the struct, no key.

The practically valuable cases beyond strings and ints:

```go
// struct keys — composite lookups
key := struct{ Region, AZ string }{"us-east", "1a"}
counts[key]++

// array keys — fixed-size sequences
var ip [4]byte
copy(ip[:], bytes)
seen[ip] = true
```

Struct keys are the underrated one: a small comparable struct gives you multi-field lookup keys without string-concatenation or nested maps. The rule is just the == rule — and the compile error for a bad key type (invalid map key type) is the language teaching it at build time.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why is == the gate? Trace the hash-table operations:

insert: hash(k) → bucket → store (k, v). The key must hash stably.
lookup: hash(k) → bucket → compare k against stored keys with ==. Equality must match hash equality.

Both operations lean on the same two properties: a stable hash and a well-defined equality that agrees with it. Slices break both: contents mutate (hash rots) and == between two slice headers checks pointer+len — not the semantics a lookup wants. Go's designers chose to exclude rather than pick a semantics (deep-equal keys would need O(n) compares per probe and a defined deep-hash) — the constraint pushes you toward strings, ints, and structs, which cover real key shapes honestly.

The mutability subtlety for struct keys: == compares FIELDS, so two struct keys with equal fields are the same key — value semantics. But if the struct contains a POINTER field, == compares the pointer, and two structs pointing at equal-but-distinct data are different keys. The key's behavior is exactly its =='s behavior — no more, no less. When that surprises, the fix is storing the data you match on (the dereferenced values) in the key, not the pointer.
